catalog_quote: L’accent de mot est un accent démarcatif, qui permet de segmenter la chaîne parlée et de repérer les unités. Il n’existe pas d’accent de syntagme, contrairement à ce qui se passe en français, par exemple. L’accent tonique primaire tombe sur la syllabe pénultième, dont il augmente l’intensité, rallonge la durée de la voyelle, et élève légèrement la hauteur. Il est accompagné, dans les mots de quatre syllabes au moins, par un accent tonique secondaire ... L’accent primaire frappe normalement la voyelle pénultième, et n’a pas de valeur contrastive. Un accent secondaire frappe également la première syllabe pour les mots de quatre syllabes ou plus, indépendamment du nombre de syllabes qui la sépare de la syllabe pénultième tonique. Cela explique que la deuxième voyelle, post-tonique, tende à se syncoper en discours rapide dans certains de ses mots longs. [p. 54] ... On a vu que l’accent primaire tombe toujours, en sun̄wadia sur la syllabe pénultième du mot. Les formes enclitiques, ne modifient pas le schéma accentuel du mot. [p. 64]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: L'accent de mot est un accent démarcatif, qui permet de segmenter la chaîne parlée et de repérer les unités. Il n'existe pas d'accent de syntagme, contrairement à ce qui se passe en français, par exemple. L'accent tonique primaire tombe sur la syllabe pénultième, dont il augmente l'intensité, rallonge la durée de la voyelle, et élève légèrement la hauteur. Il est accompagné, dans les mots de quatre syllabes au moins, par un accent tonique secondaire [...] L'accent primaire frappe normalement la voyelle pénultième, et n'a pas de valeur contrastive. Un accent secondaire frappe également la première syllabe pour les mots de quatre syllabes ou plus, indépendamment du nombre de syllabes qui la sépare de la syllabe pénultième tonique.
new_statements.translation: Word stress is a demarcative stress, which makes it possible to segment the speech chain and locate the units. There is no phrase stress, unlike what happens in French, for example. Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable, whose intensity it increases, whose vowel duration it lengthens, and whose pitch it slightly raises. It is accompanied, in words of at least four syllables, by a secondary stress [...] Primary stress normally strikes the penultimate vowel and has no contrastive value. A secondary stress also strikes the first syllable in words of four or more syllables, regardless of the number of syllables separating it from the stressed penultimate syllable.
new_statements.citation: Henri, Agnès. 2011. Le sun̄wadia: Éléments de description d'une langue du Vanuatu. Collection Linguistique de la Société de Linguistique de Paris 97. Louvain/Paris: Peeters.

Extracted PDF pp. 55-56 (printed pp. 54-55) with extracted text: §"2. Accentuation et prosodie / a. L'accent démarcatif" begins on printed p. 54 and reads exactly as quoted: "L'accent de mot est un accent démarcatif, qui permet de segmenter la chaîne parlée et de repérer les unités. Il n'existe pas d'accent de syntagme.. L'accent tonique primaire tombe sur la syllabe pénultième, dont il augmente l'intensité, rallonge la durée de la voyelle, et élève légèrement la hauteur. Il est accompagné, dans les mots de quatre syllabes au moins, par un accent toniq…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word (word = lexical base plus affixes; enclitics and proclitics are separate accentual words and do not shift stress, suffixes do: ['sawa] 'dance' vs [sa'wana] 'a dance'). Every vowel is its own syllable (no phonological diphthongs), so batau = [mba'tau]. Non-contrastive, demarcative; author notes it matches the Proto-Oceanic penultimate pattern.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of words of four or more syllables, whatever the distance to the penult: ['mbamba'rau] 'long', ['tamara'xai] 'old man', ['sosoi'xina] 'his sweat' (Tableau 8, p. 55).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) Five-syllable forms of the shape fossilised prefix ma- + CVC reduplication (makorkoroma ['makorko'roma] 'be crunchy', maqirqirina 'be wrinkled') take secondary stress on the reduplicated second syllable rather than the first; Henri proposes that a CVC-reduplicated syllable attracts intensity stress even after a prefix (p. 55). (2) Words ending in [aj]/[ej] (tamaragai, roroqai) stress the [a]/[e], phonetically the last syllable, because the glide is an allophone of /i/ and counts as the final syllable's nucleus (pp. 36-37). (3) When a word loses its final vowel by sandhi/syncope, stress moves left so as to fall again on the new penult (p. 37). Contrastive/emphatic accent (vowel lengthening + falling-rising contour) is separate from word stress (p. 55).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (base + affixes); clitics are separate accentual words (disyllabic clitics stressed on their first syllable). Explicitly no phrase-level accent. Based on auditory field data; author states no instrumental analysis was possible (fn. 15, p. 56).
new_statements.identity_note: Henri's 'sun̄wadia' is the same variety Glottolog calls Sunwadia (mari1426) = Marino / North Maewo [mrb], spoken in the north-west of Maewo; her fieldwork is on the northern variety (Codrington's Tanoriki, Ivens' Lotora are the same northern dialect area). No separate dialect glottocode involved.

new_statements.translation: Word accent is a demarcative accent [...]. The primary tonic accent falls on the penultimate syllable, whose intensity it increases, lengthening the vowel and slightly raising the pitch. In words of at least four syllables it is accompanied by a secondary tonic accent [...] The primary accent normally strikes the penultimate vowel and has no contrastive value. A secondary accent also strikes the first syllable in words of four or more syllables, regardless of the number of syllables separating it from the tonic penultimate syllable.
new_statements.citation: Henri, Agnès. 2010. Éléments de description d'une langue mélanésienne du Vanuatu, le sungwadia. PhD thesis, Université Paris-Sorbonne (Paris IV).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (fixed-unreviewed, penultimate stress, cited to Henri 2011 pp. 54-55) and the verified existing statement come from this very text; the re-read confirms fixed penultimate primary stress. Detail beyond the catalog rule string: initial secondary stress in words of 4+ syllables (so 4-syllable words are 2010, 5-syllable 20010 in a two-level notation), the reduplicated-CVC exception, and the suffix-vs-enclitic stress-shift criterion (pp. 64-65). No open copy of the 2010 thesis typescript exists to check whether its wording differs.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable, non-contrastive (realised as greater intensity, vowel lengthening and slightly raised pitch); there is no phrase-level accent. Suffixes count as part of the word and shift the stress to the new penult (sawa ['sawa] 'danser' -> sawa-na [sa'wana] 'danse'), enclitics do not.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In words of four or more syllables a secondary stress falls on the first syllable, whatever the distance to the tonic penult (Tableau 8: babarau ["mbamba'rau], tavaragata ["taf(a)ra'xata], tamaragai ["tamara'xai]); the post-tonic second vowel of such long words tends to syncopate in fast speech.
new_statements.exceptions: Five-syllable ma- prefixed verbs with a CVC reduplicant (makorkoroma ["makorko'roma] 'être croquant', maqirqirina ["makwirkwi'rina] 'être ridé') take the secondary stress on the second syllable (the reduplicated CVC) rather than the first; Henri proposes that in forms of more than three syllables with CVC reduplication the reduplicated syllable carries an intensity accent even after a prefix. Footnote 13 notes that Sun̄wadia does not show the Manam/Fijian antepenult attraction when a vowel precedes the penult vowel. A separate 'accent contrastif' (emphatic lengthening of the tonic vowel with falling-rising contour, ex. 14 No-ku kea!) is pragmatic, not lexical.
new_statements.identity_note: Henri describes Sun̄wadia (sungwadia, also Marino / North Maewo), the Oceanic language of northern Maewo Island, north-central Vanuatu, from two three-month field trips; Codrington's and Capell's 'Tanoriki' and Ivens's 'Lotora' are older village-named varieties of Maewo grouped under mari1426 by Glottolog.
